title: Continuous Random Variables
intro: A continuous random variable spreads its probability over an interval with no point carrying any. A density describes how thickly; probabilities are areas under it.

blocks.caption: A probability density function and what it computes.

blocks.text: Two consequences surprise at first. Every single point has probability zero, $P(X = x) = 0$, so it does not matter whether interval ends are included. And a density value is not a probability: it can exceed 1 (the uniform density on $[0, 0.25]$ is 4). What a density does give is probability per unit length: $P(x\le X\le x + dx)\approx f_X(x)\,dx$ for small $dx$.

The CDF is the integral of the density, $F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^xf(t)\,dt$, and where it is differentiable $f = F'$. The quantile function inverts the CDF: the $q$-quantile is the smallest $x$ with $F(x)\ge q$. The median is the 0.5-quantile, and quartiles and percentiles are the others. Quantiles are how you read off intervals and thresholds, and the quantile function is how computers sample (Transformations (#/probability/random-variables/transformations)).

Not every random variable is discrete or has a density. A waiting time that is zero with probability 0.3 (no queue) and exponential otherwise has a CDF with a jump at 0 and a density elsewhere. Stranger still, the Cantor distribution has a continuous CDF but no density at all (Measure-Theoretic Probability (#/probability/measure-theory)). The CDF handles all of these uniformly, which is why it is the general description.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad
lam = 0.5                                        # an exponential lifetime with rate 1/2 (mean 2)
f = lambda x: lam * np.exp(-lam * x)
print("total probability  =", round(quad(f, 0, np.inf)[0], 10))
print("P(1 < X < 3)       =", round(quad(f, 1, 3)[0], 6), " = e^(-0.5) - e^(-1.5) =", round(np.exp(-0.5) - np.exp(-1.5), 6))
print("density at 0       =", f(0), "(a density value, not a probability)")
print("P(X = 2) exactly   = 0; P(1.99 < X < 2.01) =", round(quad(f, 1.99, 2.01)[0], 6), "~ f(2) * 0.02 =", round(f(2) * 0.02, 6))
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
x = rng.exponential(1 / lam, 200000)
hist, edges = np.histogram(x, bins=[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 10])
for (a, b), h in zip(zip(edges, edges[1:]), hist):
    print(f"[{a:>2}, {b:>2}): simulated {h / len(x):.4f}, exact {quad(f, a, b)[0]:.4f}")
# A density bigger than 1: uniform on [0, 0.25]
print("uniform on [0, 0.25] has density", 1 / 0.25, "everywhere on its support")

blocks.text: Output of the run: the exponential density with rate 1/2 integrates to 1; $P(1 < X < 3) = e^{-0.5} - e^{-1.5} = 0.3834$; the probability of a window of width 0.02 around 2 is 0.003679, equal to $f(2)\times0.02$; and histogram frequencies of 200 000 samples match the integrals of the density over each bin to two or three decimals.

blocks.title: Median of an exponential
blocks.text: Find the median of an exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$.
solution: This is less than the mean $1/\lambda$: the long right tail pulls the mean up.

blocks.title: Probability from a CDF
blocks.text: $F(x) = 1 - 1/x^2$ for $x\ge1$ (and 0 below). Find the density and $P(2 < X\le4)$.
